title: The Church and the Ruler
lead: How should God's people relate to the rulers over them? The Bible shows kings who punished false worship, kings who overstepped into the priests' work, and faithful people who refused a ruler's command. Christians have drawn very different lessons about obedience, resistance, and whether governments should enforce religion.

sections.h: Kings, priests and false religion in Israel
sections.b: Israel's kings were not priests. When Saul offered a sacrifice himself, Samuel rebuked him (1 Samuel 13:8–14), and Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The law called for the death of those who led Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–11), and Elijah had the prophets of Baal killed (1 Kings 18:40). Good kings such as Hezekiah and Josiah tore down idols and shrines (2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 23:4–20). Christians differ on whether these laws, given to Israel as a nation under God, guide governments today.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 13:8–14; 2 Chronicles 26:16–21; Deuteronomy 13:1–11; 1 Kings 18:40; 2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 23:4–20

sections.b: The Hebrew midwives would not kill the baby boys as Pharaoh ordered (Exodus 1:17). David refused to harm Saul, "the LORD's anointed," even when Saul hunted him (1 Samuel 24:6). Mordecai would not bow to Haman (Esther 3:2), and Daniel and his friends refused to worship the king's image or stop praying (Daniel 3:16–18; Daniel 6:10). Jesus said to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar and God what belongs to God (Mark 12:17). Paul told believers to submit to the governing authorities as God's servants (Romans 13:1–7), and Peter said to honor the emperor (1 Peter 2:13–17). Yet the apostles told the council, "We must obey God rather than people" (Acts 5:29), and Revelation pictures a state that demands worship as a beast (Revelation 13).

sections.b: For many centuries most churches held that rulers should protect true religion and punish heresy. Orthodox tradition speaks of a harmony, symphonia, between church and empire. The Catholic Church long taught that the state should support the true faith; the Second Vatican Council (1965) declared that every person has a right to religious freedom. The original Westminster Confession gave the magistrate a duty to suppress heresy; American Presbyterians revised it in 1788. Lutherans teach two kingdoms: God rules the world through the sword of government and the church through the gospel. Anglicans have the monarch as the church's supreme governor in England. Anabaptists held that the sword belongs outside the perfection of Christ, and Baptists such as Roger Williams argued that no government should force anyone's conscience.

sections.h: May Christians resist an unjust ruler?
sections.b: Early Christians suffered under hostile emperors without taking up arms. Medieval and Reformation thinkers debated whether a tyrant could be resisted. The Church of England's homily against rebellion (1570) and many royalists pointed to David sparing Saul. Calvin allowed lower officials to restrain a tyrant, and Samuel Rutherford's Lex, Rex (1644) argued that the king is under the law. Catholic teaching allows resistance to grave and lasting tyranny only as a last resort. Anabaptists, Quakers and many Mennonites practice nonviolent refusal. Jehovah's Witnesses stay politically neutral and refuse to salute flags, which they count as idolatry. Most Christians agree that believers must refuse a command to sin, even when they disagree on how far further resistance may go.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 26:9–11; Acts 5:29; Romans 13:1–7; Daniel 3:16–18; Exodus 1:17

common: Christians agree that believers should pray for their rulers and must not obey a command to worship another god.
uncommon: A few Christians, called theonomists, argue that modern governments should enforce the civil laws of Moses.
